title: Design and additive manufacturing of nonlinear graded joints between austenitic and ferritic-martensitic steels - Scientific Reports
byline: Nandwana; Peeyush; Kannan; Rangasayee; Nayir; Selda; Jordan; Brian; Wang; Hong; Sridharan; Niyanth; Srivastava; Ankit
html:
Abstract

Welds between austenitic stainless (SS347H) and ferritic-martensitic (P91) steels are commonly used in power-generation systems. However, differences in their properties, such as thermal expansion coefficients and carbon chemical potentials, often lead to premature failure. While additive manufacturing (AM) of compositionally graded transition joints (GTJs) offers a promising solution, most prior efforts have relied on linear composition gradients, which can be suboptimal. In this work, we use thermo-kinetic modeling to design, and blown powder directed energy deposition (BP–DED) to fabricate, a nonlinear GTJ between the two steels. The CALPHAD calculations show that nonlinear composition gradients reduce carbon chemical potential gradients across the joint compared to linear composition gradients thereby enhancing thermal stability of the joint. The fabricated nonlinear joint exhibited an average yield strength of \(\:478\pm\:16\:\text{M}\text{P}\text{a}\), comparable to or exceeding that of the two base materials. Pressurized creep testing on a tubular assembly comprising of GTJ welded to SS347H and P91 on either side showed failure after \(\:967\) hours in the P91 region, while the nonlinear GTJ remained intact. This approach provides a pathway for designing high-performance nonlinear GTJs for other technologically critical material systems.

Introduction

Dissimilar metal welds between austenitic stainless and ferritic-martensitic steels are used in the superheater section of power generation plants, with austenitic stainless steels employed in higher-temperature regions and ferritic-martensitic steels in lower-temperature regions. While austenitic stainless steels offer superior corrosion and creep resistance, ferritic-martensitic steels are used in lower-temperature zones due to their significantly lower cost and acceptable performance under those conditions1,2. Dak and Pandey have provided a comprehensive review on welding of austenitic and ferritic-martensitic steels3. These dissimilar metal welds prematurely fail primarily because of (a) mismatch in coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) leading to high interfacial stresses during repeated thermal cycling, and (b) carbon migration across the interface resulting from carbon chemical potential differences between the two steels3,4.

Graded transition joints (GTJs) are a class of functionally graded materials (FGMs) which rely on gradual changes in composition and properties to mitigate premature failure unlike dissimilar metal welds that have sharp transitions. FGMs were first explored in 1980s for thermal barrier coatings and were largely limited to metal – ceramic composites5,6. Advances in additive manufacturing (AM) techniques like blown powder directed energy deposition (BP–DED) and wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) have accelerated research in metallic FGMs. It should be noted that the rate and distance over which composition can be varied depends on the resolution of the manufacturing technique. While WAAM and gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW) can fabricate large parts, their compositional resolution along the build direction is limited by their typical layer heights of 1–4 mm and by partial dilution resulting from re-melting of layers whereas the in-plane resolution is affected by the melt pool dimensions6. In contrast, BP-DED has smaller layer thickness and melt pool dimensions which can enable more precise compositional control over shorter build heights.

Fabrication of metallic GTJs is challenging because the intermediate compositions may form brittle intermetallic phases, have porosity, enter hot or solidification cracking regimes, and develop high residual stresses. Additionally, post-fabrication heat treatments optimized for one alloy maybe incompatible with the variable composition profile of the transition joint6,7. Addressing these challenges is critical for additively manufactured GTJs to replace dissimilar metal welds between austenitic and ferritic/martensitic steels in power plants.

One of the earliest studies on austenitic – ferritic/martensitic GTJs, conducted by Brentrup and DuPont, utilized gas GTAW with dual wires and varying feed rates to fabricate a \(\:50\:\text{m}\text{m}\) long transition joint2. Subsequently, Sridharan et al. used BP–DED to fabricate a GTJ with \(\:20\%\) composition increments, followed by Zuback et al. who refined this approach by using \(\:10\%\) increments4,8. More recently, Galler et al. performed a systematic design of GTJs through thermodynamic and kinetic modeling for various filler combinations, which were then fabricated using GTAW9.

Most AM-fabricated GTJs reported to date employ linear composition gradients i.e., constant composition increments, which are easier to fabricate but maybe suboptimal when both CTE mismatch and carbon chemical potential differences must be mitigated simultaneously. In practice, such gradients are fabricated as discrete composition segments, and the effective transition can be further broadened by dilution during AM. The objective of this study is to (i) design a nonlinear GTJ between a \(\:9\%\) Cr ferritic-martensitic steel (P91) and an austenitic stainless steel (SS347H), (ii) fabricate the GTJ and characterize the phase evolution across the joint, and (iii) establish baseline mechanical performance via room temperature tensile testing and pressurized creep testing under simulated operating conditions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of design and fabrication of a nonlinear GTJ between these two materials.

Thermo-Calc™ was used to design the nonlinear GTJ to minimize the CTE and carbon chemical potential differences by identifying inflection points in these properties with changing composition within the transition joint. This resulted in discrete composition steps that change in a nonlinear fashion across the length of the joint unlike the constant increments in a linear transition joint. BP-DED was used to fabricate the nonlinear GTJ which was subsequently subjected to microscopic examination for phase evolution across the joint. Tensile testing coupled with digital image correlation (DIC) was conducted to determine the room temperature behavior of the GTJ in as-fabricated condition. Additionally, the GTJ was welded to SS347H and P91 tubes on either end for conducting pressurized creep testing under simulated operating conditions to evaluate the integrity of the GTJ during service. The following sections discuss the key findings and underpinning mechanisms driving the microstructure evolution and mechanical behavior.

Results and discussions

The process flow for design, fabrication and characterization of the nonlinear GTJ in this study is summarized in Fig. 1. The primary driver for the design of the GTJ was mitigation of CTE differences calculated using CALPHAD which formed the basis for the choice of composition gradients within the joint. Subsequently, variations in carbon chemical potential gradients and carbon concentration changes during simulated thermal aging were calculated as a function of transition joint length. The thermo-kinetic calculations coupled with the limitations in printing resolution of BP-DED were used to determine the optimal transition joint length to be printed. Post fabrication, the transition joint was subjected to detailed microstructure and mechanical characterization. The following sections present a detailed discussion on the design, fabrication, and characterization of the nonlinear GTJ in this study.

Schematic depiction of the process flow for design, fabrication, and testing of the nonlinear GTJ in this study.

Design of nonlinear GTJ

The computed CTE at the desired service temperature of \(650\ \!^\circ\text{C}\) as a function of increasing SS347H mass fraction at room temperature is shown in Fig. 2 (a). There are specific inflection points where CTE changes while remaining largely unchanged over a range of compositions. Both, the linear and nonlinear joints will encounter these CTE changes, which while abrupt, are less steep than in a dissimilar metal weld with sharp transitions. As a result, selecting compositions that coincide with CTE changes will make the fabrication of joint more strategic and cost effective over a linear transition joint while providing a smoother CTE gradient compared to a dissimilar metal weld. These inflection points in CTE yield nonlinear composition increments for the transition joint. This approach contrasts with that used by the earlier researchers where the focus was minimization of carbon chemical potential gradient by using linear composition grading over longer joint lengths compared to a typical dissimilar metal weld2,4,8,9.

For subsequent calculations of carbon chemical potential gradients and carbon concentration gradients across the transition joint, in addition to the nonlinear GTJ, a linear GTJ with constant 10% increments in SS347H or consequently, 10% decrements in P91 was used as a baseline. For example, for a \(20\text{ mm}\) long joint with linear composition increments, this corresponds to a decrease in P91 content by \(\:10\%\) approximately every \(2.22\text{ mm}\). In contrast, the nonlinear GTJ resulted in fewer steps with variable composition changes at every step: from \(\:80\%\:\to\:\:60\%\:\to\:\:50\%\:\to\:\:40\%\:\to\:\:20\%\) P91 distributed at uniform spatial intervals. For a \(\:20\:\text{m}\text{m}\) long joint, this corresponds to a decrease in P91 content approximately every \(4\text{ mm}\). As such, unlike the linear GTJ, the nonlinear design places fewer but strategically selected compositions to better respond to localized variations in phase stability, carbon chemical potential, and thermal expansion behavior.

The calculated variation in carbon chemical potential across the GTJ for transition zone lengths ranging from \(5\text{ mm}\) to \(20\text{ mm}\) after simulated aging at \(650\ \!^\circ\text{C}\) for \(100,000\text{ hours}\) is shown in Fig. 2(b). The variations in carbon chemical potential across the joint are presented for both linear and nonlinear GTJs. In these figures, vertical dashed lines denote the transition zone boundaries, with the dashed line at \(10\text{ mm}\) marking the interface between the \(\:100\%\) P91 region and the start of the transition zone. In all cases, the carbon chemical potential initially decreases gradually as we move away from the \(\:100\%\) P91 region into the transition zone, followed by a rapid drop. For the \(5\text{ mm}\) transition zone, this rapid drop in chemical potential extends into the \(\:100\%\) SS347H region, whereas in the \(12.5\text{ mm}\) and \(20\text{ mm}\) transition zones, the rapid drop ends within the transition zone, near the boundary with the \(\:100\%\) SS347H region. Beyond this point, there is a more gradual decrease, eventually saturating at the carbon chemical potential value of the \(\:100\%\) SS347H base material. For these longer transition zones, the carbon chemical potential from near the P91–GTJ interface to more than half the length of the GTJ is notably lower for the nonlinear GTJ compared to the linear GTJ. This difference in carbon chemical potential between linear and nonlinear GTJs becomes more pronounced as the transition zone length increases from \(\:12.5\) to \(20\text{ mm}\) thereby highlighting the potential for improved service life of the nonlinear GTJ.

The variation of the carbon concentration across the GTJs before and after simulated aging at \(650\ \!^\circ\text{C}\) for \(100,000\text{ hours}\) is shown in Fig. 2(c). Again, vertical dashed lines denote the transition zone boundaries. For both linear and nonlinear GTJs, the post-aging variation of carbon content from the \(\:100\%\) P91 region to the \(\:100\%\) SS347H region deviates from the initial design. In both cases, as expected, carbon is depleted in the \(\:100\%\) P91 region near the GTJ boundary and enriched on the \(\:100\%\) SS347H side. The predicted post-aging carbon concentration first decreases from well within the \(\:100\%\) P91 region into the GTJ, then increases, and finally undergoes a continuous decrease until it levels off in the SS347H region. The extent of carbon depletion in the \(\:100\%\) P91 region, relative to the initial value, decreases with increasing GTJ length for both linear and nonlinear designs. However, the nonlinear GTJs exhibit a much smoother variation in carbon content from the \(\:100\%\) P91 region into the GTJ.

(a) Variation of calculated CTE with increasing fraction of SS347H with vertical dashed lines indicating inflection points in CTE that resulted in a nonlinear composition profile of the GTJ (b) Carbon chemical potential across linear and nonlinear GTJs with transition joint lengths ranging from \(\:5\) to \(20\text{ mm}\). (c) Initial and final carbon concentration profiles after simulated aging at \(650\ \!^\circ\text{C}\) for 100,000 hours across linear and nonlinear GTJs of varying lengths.

Microstructure evolution in BP-DED fabricated nonlinear GTJ

Based on the thermo-kinetic calculations, a nonlinear GTJ wall with 12.5 mm transition zone was deposited using the BeAM Modulo BP-DED system as shown in Fig. 1 (refer to Methods for details of the deposition process). Owing to the higher cost of AM, the smallest transition zone length that results in lower carbon chemical potential gradient compared to a linear transition joint was chosen. Note that in a production scenario, the lower bounds of transition joint length will be dictated by the resolution of the machine in terms of layer thickness as well as the ability to switch powder flow rates to reliably achieve the desired composition increments whereas the upper limit is dictated by the build time and deposition rates.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analyses were conducted across the entire sample to evaluate texture and phase evolution in different regions, with the results summarized in Fig. 3. The macro-scale inverse pole figure (IPF) maps in Fig. 3(a) show a coarse ferritic microstructure in the P91 section, a refined ferritic/martensitic structure in the transition zone, and a coarse austenitic microstructure in the SS347H region.

The pole figure maps in Fig. 3(b), extracted from representative areas of the macro-scale IPF map, indicate that P91 exhibits a weak (\(\:2\times\:\) random) \(\left\langle {001} \right\rangle \:\) texture, the transition zone develops a strong (\(\:7\times\:\) random) \(\left\langle {001} \right\rangle\) texture, and SS347H shows an unexpected \(\left\langle {011} \right\rangle\) texture (\(\:3.1\times\:\) random). High-resolution IPF maps from selected regions (marked by boxes in Fig. 3a) further reveal that the P91 region consists of coarse \(\:\delta\:\)-ferrite grains instead of a martensitic \(\:\left(\alpha\:{\prime\:}\right)\) microstructure. Lyu et al.10 also reported large volume fraction of δ-ferrite in P91 steel fabricated using BP-DED whereas Mahmud et al.11 reported a fully martensitic structure for P91 with relatively higher Cr content, fabricated using BP-DED which highlights the role of powder composition, process parameters and consequently, thermal history on microstructure evolution during BP-DED. The high-resolution IPF maps also show that the transition zone at \(\:50\%\) P91 region contains a fine martensitic structure as opposed to an expected mixture of martensite and austenite while the SS347H region consists of coarse austenite \(\:\left(\gamma\:\right)\) grains as expected.

The phase map in Fig. 3(c) shows that the transition zone is predominantly ferritic/martensitic but gradually transforms into a dual-phase ferritic–austenitic microstructure in the \(\:20\%\) P91 region. These observations contrast with the designed phase distribution predicted by thermodynamic calculations, likely due to non-equilibrium solidification and rapid cooling rates inherent to AM.
